idiom_name: POSIX sem_t with sem_init / sem_wait / sem_post
implementation_notes: POSIX semaphores are the C realization: sem_init(&s, pshared, N) creates an unnamed semaphore in memory (pshared=1 places it in a shared memory region so other processes can use it), sem_wait() blocks while the count is zero and then decrements, sem_post() returns a permit, and sem_trywait()/sem_timedwait() bound the wait instead of blocking forever. Named semaphores (sem_open/sem_close/sem_unlink) are kernel-persistent and shared by name across processes. The hand-written counter plus mutex and condition variable is only justified when POSIX semaphores are unavailable (bare-metal or pre-POSIX platforms) or when the wait must be integrated into a custom scheduler; link with -pthread, and remember sem_wait() is a cancellation point that can also fail with EINTR and must be retried.
pitfalls: sem_wait() can be interrupted by a signal (EINTR); treating that failure as 'no permit available' is a classic bug, and the loop must retry.
A thread-shared sem_init semaphore must outlive every user; destroying it while another thread is blocked in sem_wait() is undefined behaviour.
sem_post() is async-signal-safe and may be called from a handler, but sem_wait() is not - only the release side of the pattern can live in signal context.

variants.name: Hand-rolled mutex + condition variable
variants.idiom_name: pthread_mutex_t + pthread_cond_t counter and waiter loop
variants.implementation_notes: When POSIX semaphores are not available, the same pattern is built from a mutex, a condition variable and an integer count: acquire locks the mutex and loops while count == 0 on pthread_cond_wait(), release increments the count and signals one waiter. The wait must be a while loop (pthread_cond_wait can wake spuriously and the mutex is re-acquired on return), and pthread_cond_timedwait() gives the bounded-wait form. This is the manual realization: it adds the release/acquire bookkeeping that sem_t already provides, so prefer sem_t whenever the platform has it.
pitfalls: Using if instead of while around pthread_cond_wait() breaks on spurious wakeups and on signals stolen by another waiter.
Signalling while holding the mutex is correct but can cause a thundering herd and priority inversion; unlocking before signal() is often preferable.
Forgetting that pthread_cond_wait() re-acquires the mutex before returning, so code after the loop must assume the lock is held.
